items.title: 250 GD Topics
items.summary: A big list of group discussion topics to practise.
items.body: Pick 3 topics a day. Speak for 2 minutes on each, then ask Tushar AI to score you in Practice Lab.

items.title: 50 GD Topics with Detail
items.body: Read the points first, then practise your own opening and conclusion. The file downloads to your phone.

items.title: Amul: a brand built on a cooperative
items.summary: How a farmer cooperative competed with multinationals and won on trust and price.
items.body:
**Background**
Amul grew out of the dairy cooperative movement in Anand, Gujarat. Farmers owned the business, so milk was collected, processed and sold without a layer of middlemen.

**What worked**
- Value pricing: affordable products for mass households.
- One umbrella brand across butter, milk, cheese and ice cream.
- The Amul girl hoardings, running since 1966, comment on current events every few weeks. The ads cost little and stay in public memory.

**Lessons**
- Distribution and trust can be a stronger moat than ad budgets.
- Consistency of a single creative idea compounds over decades.

**Discuss**
1. What risks come with topical advertising?
2. How would you extend Amul into a premium segment without hurting the core brand?
3. Is a cooperative structure a strength or a limit when scaling?

items.title: Tata Nano: when positioning backfires
items.summary: A very low-priced car that struggled because of how it was perceived.
items.body:
**Background**
Launched in 2008, the Nano was pitched as an affordable car for families moving up from two-wheelers, with a headline price of around one lakh rupees.

**What went wrong**
- The 'cheapest car' label made buyers feel it signalled low status.
- Aspirational buyers wanted a car that showed they had progressed, not one that showed they had saved.
- Early publicity about quality and safety concerns hurt trust.

**Lessons**
- Price is part of positioning, not the whole of it.
- Customers buy identity as well as function.

**Discuss**
1. How would you reposition the Nano today?
2. Which segment should it have targeted first?
3. Compare with a brand that made 'value' feel aspirational.

items.title: Kodak: the cost of ignoring disruption
items.summary: An early digital camera inventor that protected its film business too long.
items.body:
**Background**
Kodak engineers built an early digital camera in 1975. The company dominated film and the profitable chemicals and paper that went with it.

**What went wrong**
- Digital threatened the core business, so leadership held back.
- Rivals and phones moved the market while Kodak stayed attached to film margins.
- Kodak filed for bankruptcy protection in 2012.

**Lessons**
- Cannibalise yourself before someone else does.
- Define the business by the customer need (preserving memories), not the product (film).

**Discuss**
1. Which framework explains this best: Ansoff, BCG, or disruptive innovation?
2. What would you have done in 2000?

items.title: Quick commerce: is it sustainable?
items.summary: A discussion case on 10-minute delivery, unit economics and urban demand.
items.body:
**Context**
Quick commerce platforms promise delivery in minutes using small local warehouses (dark stores) in dense neighbourhoods.

**Questions to think about**
- Unit economics: delivery cost, order value, discounts and warehouse rent.
- Where does profit come from: higher basket size, advertising from brands, private labels, or fees?
- Customer behaviour: convenience for top-up purchases versus planned grocery shopping.
- Gig workers: safety, pay and regulation.

**Frameworks to use**
Porter's Five Forces, a simple unit economics table, and a SWOT of one platform.

**Discuss**
1. Will this model work outside the top cities?
2. Who wins if competition continues: platforms, brands or customers?

Tip: use recent news to update your facts before a GD or interview.

items.title: Marketing Management Trainee (sample)
items.summary: Typical FMCG or consumer brand trainee role. Use it to practise CV tailoring.
items.body:
**Role**
Support the brand team with campaign planning, consumer research and sales coordination.

**Responsibilities**
- Assist in preparing brand plans and monthly performance reviews.
- Analyse market share, pricing and competitor activity.
- Coordinate with agencies and the sales team on launches.
- Present insights to category managers.

**Skills they look for**
Analytical thinking, communication, Excel, curiosity about consumers, ownership.

**Keywords for your CV**
consumer insight, market share, campaign, A/B test, go-to-market, brand positioning.

**Try this**
Paste your CV into CV Lab with this JD for a tailored score.

items.title: Business Analyst (sample)
items.summary: A common consulting or tech role built around structured problem solving.
items.body:
**Role**
Work with clients and internal teams to define problems, analyse data and recommend actions.

**Responsibilities**
- Gather requirements and map business processes.
- Build dashboards and reports in Excel, SQL or BI tools.
- Prepare slides summarising findings for stakeholders.
- Track KPIs and flag risks.

**Skills they look for**
Structured thinking, Excel, basic SQL, storytelling with data, stakeholder management.

**Keywords for your CV**
KPI, process improvement, dashboard, requirement gathering, cost reduction, stakeholder.

**Try this**
Rewrite two CV bullets with numbers: 'Improved X by Y% by doing Z.'

items.title: Sales Management Trainee (sample)
items.summary: Field-and-office sales role with targets, distributors and key accounts.
items.body:
**Role**
Own sales targets for a region or key accounts and grow distribution.

**Responsibilities**
- Plan monthly sales targets and track achievement.
- Manage distributors, retailers or key accounts.
- Run trade promotions and monitor stock.
- Report market feedback to the marketing team.

**Skills they look for**
Negotiation, resilience, communication, comfort with travel and targets.

**Keywords for your CV**
target achievement, distribution, channel, negotiation, key account, trade promotion.

**Try this**
Prepare a story where you hit a hard target using the STAR method.

items.title: Tell me about yourself: a simple structure
items.summary: Use Present, Past, Future in about 90 seconds.
items.body:
**Structure**
1. Present: who you are now (MBA student, specialisation, one headline strength).
2. Past: two or three experiences that built that strength (work, projects, leadership).
3. Future: what you want next and why this role or company fits.

**Tips**
- Keep it under 90 seconds.
- End with a hook the interviewer can ask about.
- Avoid reciting your CV line by line.
- Practise out loud and record yourself.

**Try this**
Open Practice Lab, start a Personal Interview and answer the first question using this structure.

items.title: STAR method for behavioural questions
items.summary: Answer 'tell me about a time when...' clearly and with results.
items.body:
**STAR**
- Situation: set the scene in one or two sentences.
- Task: what was your responsibility?
- Action: what you did, step by step (use 'I', not 'we').
- Result: the outcome with a number if possible, and what you learned.

**Stories to prepare**
Leadership, conflict in a team, failure, tight deadline, persuading someone, taking initiative.

**Common mistake**
Spending 80% on the situation and rushing the result. Aim for 20% setup, 50% action, 30% result.

items.title: Why MBA? Why this company? Weaknesses
items.summary: Honest, specific answers to the three questions almost everyone gets.
items.body:
**Why MBA**
Link a specific gap (for example, finance or strategy skills) to a specific goal. Avoid 'for growth' or 'for a better salary'.

**Why this company**
Name one product, one recent initiative and one value that matches you. Show you did the research.

**Your weakness**
Pick a real but fixable weakness, show what you are doing about it, and show progress. Do not pick a disguised strength like 'I work too hard'.

**Try this**
Write each answer in three sentences, then say it aloud in 30 seconds.

items.title: STP and the 4Ps
items.summary: The base framework for almost any marketing question.
items.body:
**STP**
- Segmentation: divide the market by demographics, behaviour, needs or geography.
- Targeting: choose the segment(s) with the best fit and potential.
- Positioning: the place your brand holds in the customer's mind.

**4Ps**
- Product: features, quality, brand, packaging.
- Price: pricing strategy, discounts, value perception.
- Place: channels and distribution.
- Promotion: advertising, PR, digital, sales promotion.

**Use it**
Start with STP, then design the 4Ps to support the positioning. Mention extended Ps (people, process, physical evidence) for services.

items.title: Porter's Five Forces
items.summary: A quick way to judge how attractive an industry is.
items.body:
**The five forces**
1. Threat of new entrants: barriers like capital, brand, regulation.
2. Bargaining power of suppliers.
3. Bargaining power of buyers.
4. Threat of substitutes.
5. Rivalry among existing competitors.

**How to use it**
Rate each force high, medium or low with one reason, then conclude whether the industry is attractive and what a firm should do.

**Example prompt**
Apply the five forces to Indian quick commerce or electric two-wheelers.

items.title: BCG matrix
items.summary: Classify products by market growth and market share.
items.body:
**Quadrants**
- Stars: high growth, high share. Invest to keep leadership.
- Cash cows: low growth, high share. Harvest the cash.
- Question marks: high growth, low share. Invest selectively or exit.
- Dogs: low growth, low share. Fix or divest.

**Limits**
Market share and growth are not the only drivers of success. Definitions of 'market' can change the result.

**Try this**
Place three products from one company (for example, a consumer goods firm) on the matrix and justify each.

items.title: Ansoff matrix
items.summary: Four growth routes by combining products and markets.
items.body:
**Growth routes**
- Market penetration: existing products, existing markets (lowest risk).
- Market development: existing products, new markets.
- Product development: new products, existing markets.
- Diversification: new products, new markets (highest risk).

**Use it**
Recommend the lowest-risk route that meets the growth target, and say what would justify moving to a riskier one.

**Try this**
Choose a brand you know and give one example of each route.
